questions.q: What specific failure mode do Named Credentials exist to remove?
options: Slow callout response times
The inability to call any external system from Apex at all
A credential value hardcoded directly in Apex code, visible to anyone who can read that code and hard to rotate everywhere it's used
The 15-minute Apex transaction time limit
questions.explain: Named Credentials get authentication details out of Apex entirely -- the credential's value is never visible to the Apex code, which directly removes the hardcoded-credential failure mode from Lesson 1's attack chain.

questions.q: In the current Named Credentials model, what is the functional difference between an External Credential and a Named Credential?
options: The External Credential holds the authentication protocol and principals; the Named Credential holds the callout endpoint URL and points at an External Credential
They are two names for the exact same object with no functional difference
The Named Credential holds the secret material; the External Credential holds nothing but a label
External Credentials are only used for inbound calls, Named Credentials only for outbound
questions.explain: Splitting the two separates 'how we authenticate' (External Credential) from 'what endpoint we're calling' (Named Credential), letting one External Credential be reused across multiple endpoints on the same external system.

questions.q: An integration needs each individual Salesforce user to be recognized and access-controlled as themselves on the external system, mirroring their own login there. Which principal type fits, per this lesson?
options: Named Principal, because it's simpler to set up
Neither -- this scenario requires a hardcoded credential
Named Principal, because it automatically restricts each user to their own data
Per-User, because the external system needs to know and enforce access by the actual human behind the request
questions.explain: Per-User principals authenticate each Salesforce user with their own individual credential, which is exactly what's needed when the external system must distinguish between users rather than treat every call as coming from one shared service identity.

questions.q: What actually determines which users are allowed to have their callouts authenticate through a given principal?
options: Whichever user happens to be logged in gets automatic access to every principal in the org
The principal's association with specific permission sets (or permission set groups), under External Credential Principal Access
Named Credentials are available to every user in the org with no restriction possible
Only System Administrator profile users can ever use any principal
questions.explain: A principal is gated by permission-set assignment via External Credential Principal Access -- the same governance mechanism used for other access decisions, not a separate side door.

questions.q: This lesson says Named Credentials don't automatically fix one specific risk. What is it?
options: Named Credentials automatically scope the underlying identity to least privilege -- there is no remaining risk
Named Credentials cannot be used with OAuth at all
A Named Principal pointed at an over-privileged integration user is still over-privileged; Named Credentials only stop the credential from living in Apex code
Named Credentials prevent any callout from ever failing
questions.explain: Named Credentials solve where the credential lives and how authentication happens -- they say nothing about whether the identity behind the principal is well-scoped, which is exactly what Lessons 5 and 6 address next.
